To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the rate of reinforcement in a component of a multiple schedule affects resistance to extinction of behavior, and 2) resistance to extinction is higher when the component with the higher rate of reinforcement has been associated with that rate for more sessions.

resistance to extinction in multiple schedules is a power function of reinforcement rate in a component and that resistance to change is a function of how recently reinforcement rates in a component changed.

Behavioral momentum theory suggests that resistance to change of behavior is a function of the strength of the Pavlovian relation between discriminative stimuli and reinforcers that are obtained in the presence of those discriminative stimuli.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of Pavlovian conditioning in shaping the resistance to extinction of instrumental behavior.
the development of a quantitative model of behavior.
the effects of the Pavlovian relation between a discriminant stimulus (e.g., the presence of a light) and a reinforcing consequence (e.g., food) on resistance to change in operant behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
resistance to change is related to a stimulus-reinforcement relation, and that the stimulus-reinforcement relationship is a function of the history of reinforcers in the situation.
resistance to change is a function of the mass of behavior accumulated in each component of a multiple schedule.
resistance to change is related to recently reinforced behavior, but only if that behavior is associated with specific discriminative-stimuli for some period of time.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the stimulus-reinforcer relationship is a function of the rate of reinforcement and the length of time the relationship is experienced.

resistance to change is a function of the strength of the stimulus-reinforcer association, and the strength of the association is a function of both the number of sessions that the association is in effect and the rate of reinforcement.
behavioral momentum and mass-like aspects of behavior are not the same.
The main takeaway from our work is that
resistance to change is not an all-or-nothing phenomenon, but rather a gradual function of time.
it is important to examine the stimulus-reinforcer relations in multiple schedules over longer periods of time than has previously been done.
the stimulus-reinforcer relationship is important in understanding the resistance to change in operant behavior.
